subject: truncated normal log prob contour plot

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: truncated normal log prob contour plot
parts:
I've attached a log probability contour plot
for the truncated_normal model given around 500
data points simulated with y ~ normal(mu=0,sigma=1)
plus rejection sampling to make sure they have
y < 0.

There seems to be some big wide open spaces around
the true values of mu=0, sigma=1 heading positive
on mu and sigma.

So maybe the model's doing the right thing here and
the Bayesian estimator (posterior mean) is actually
pretty far away from the MAP estimate (which according
the log probs in the quadrature is right where it
should be at mu=0, sigma=1 [give or take .1 for the
data variation]).

- Bob

reasonably accurate.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] truncated normal log prob contour plot

On 9/5/12 2:50 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> One way to check if this is doing the right thing with a model this
> small would be to check against a large importance sample. 10^6
> samples (or even more) would be easy to draw and weight and should be
> reasonably accurate.

Funny. Daniel and I were just discussing directly
estimating the posterior mean using the quadrature values.

But given the contour plot, I'm pretty happy with where
we're at. I don't think it's a bug in Stan (other than the
sign bug in truncation we're about to fix in 1.0.1).

Andrew's advice in the 2nd edition of BDA (assuming he wrote
that bit) is to do quadrature and then sample directly.
I don't know if that advice will be updated for the
3rd Edition, which is pretty far along already (and includes
both Stan and HMC sections).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] truncated normal log prob contour plot
parts:
On 9/5/12 4:59 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Hmmm. I get the same contours as you but the gradients look weird (each arrow on the
> plot is the direction of the gradient with lengths relative to the gradient magnitudes.

Cool -- I thought you might've meant something
like that. Does anyone have an example of code for
making a plot like this in R?

Given the contour plot, the gradients seem OK and
they shrink around the mode near (0,1). I always
forget just how much posterior dependence there can
be in a model like this, but it totally makes sense
because a high variance gives you more leeway in the
mean estimate.

If you fix either parameter to the true value, the
other parameter gets estimated very tightly (especially
the mean with fixed variance).
>Iit does look like you could run off to nowhere (mu, sigma -> \infty) if you hit that quadratic boundary.

Luckily, the sampler doesn't run off to infinity.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] truncated normal log prob contour plot
parts:
I'm just worried about the right portion of the quadratic boundary. It looks unstable, such that a trajectory coming from the right would be attracted to the parabola but then be pushed up and to the right towards infinity. Or at the very least, if the gradients vanish on the parabola then an unlucky momentum could cause problems.

In any case, the parabola implies something like sigma = (x - mu)^{2} + const when we should have sigma^{2} = (x - \mu)^{2}+ const, no?. Are you returning the transformed variable here?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] truncated normal log prob contour plot
parts:
Each momentum dimension is initialized
independently using a unit normal.

It might be feasible to specify momenta on
the constrained parameters and then transform
to momenta on the unconstrained params. I
haven't thought it through, though, and there
are constraints because of the change in
dimensionality (e.g., with the simplex or
covariance matrices).

- Bob
